newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Port of Tauranga sees good profit growth.
newsitem.headline: Port of Tauranga sees good profit growth.

text.p: Port of Tauranga Ltd chief executive John Halling said on Wednesday he expects the company to report significantly higher profits in the 1996/97 year.
"We believe we will have a significant improvement of profitability in the coming year," Halling told a briefing of journalists.
He declined to provide specific forecasts.
On Monday, the company reported a net profit of $9.05 million in the June year against $6.03 million the previous year.

The company's share price has gained steeply since the company's result and news last week that a Fletcher Challenge Ltd-led consortium had won the bidding to buy Forestry Corp of New Zealand with its vast central North Island forests.
The share price rose from $1.77 to $2.04 on Tuesday before slipping back to $2.00 on Wednesday.
The company expects to get significant benefits from the Fletcher-FCNZ deal and may be able to delay a $8-12 million capital cost in the port's expansion plans as a result.
Halling said that only having two major forestry companies may allow Port of Tauranga to smooth the flow of logging shipments from the port.
The log berth is used only at around 52 percent capacity but at present the flow is lumpy, Halling said.
He said log exports may increase as well as FCL re-evaluates the maturity profile of the logs in its forests.
"A possible outcome is the reduction in the maturity of the trees it harvests," Halling said.
However, he added that Fletcher would not want to over-sell the log market.
Port of Tauranga expects log tonnages to exceed 3.0 million tonnes this year against 2.9 million last year and they could rise over 4.0 million tonnes.
The port company is also reviewing upwards its tariffs, which have more than halved in real terms since 1989.
Port of Tauranga rates its log handling facilities as the best in the world in terms of turnaround times and costs.
Infratil which recently increased its stake to 22 percent from 21 percent, has shown no desire for board representation, chairman Fraser McKenzie said.
The company is 55.1 percent owned by the Bay of Plenty Regional Council.
